Hi Nico,

It's been ages! I've been meaning to write to you for months, but life has been crazy.

So, the big news: I've changed jobs. I left the bank in March and I've been working at a tech startup since April. I love it, although I've been working much longer hours lately. I've also moved to a new flat in Chapinero, and I've been decorating it slowly — very slowly!

Do you remember that when we last met, I had just broken up with Sergio? Well, a few months later, I met someone new at a friend's wedding. We've been seeing each other for six months now, and I think you'd really like him.

What about you? Have you finished your master's? Have you been travelling as much as you planned? I saw on Instagram that you went to Peru in July. It looked amazing!

Let's meet soon. I've just bought a coffee machine, so you have no excuse.

Hugs,
Laura

6.title: Can we trust the news?
6.brief: Write an essay about whether people can trust the news they read on social media. Refer to recent changes and give examples.
6.briefEs: Escribe un ensayo sobre si podemos confiar en las noticias de redes sociales, con ejemplos recientes.
criteria: Present perfect for recent changes and simple past for specific examples.
One present perfect continuous to describe an ongoing trend.
Four words from the unit: biased, eyewitness, to take with a pinch of salt, to get to the bottom of.
6.model:
Over the last decade, the way people consume news has changed dramatically. Most young people no longer read newspapers; instead, they get their information from social media. This raises an important question: can we trust what we read there?

On the positive side, social media has made information more democratic. Ordinary people have become eyewitnesses who can share events in real time. During the protests in Colombia in 2021, for example, citizens posted videos that traditional media had ignored.

However, the problems are serious. False stories have been spreading faster than ever, and algorithms have been showing people only the content that confirms their opinions. Much of what we see is biased or unsubstantiated. In 2016, a fake story about the Pope supporting Donald Trump was shared almost a million times before anyone checked it.

In my opinion, we should take everything we read online with a pinch of salt. Before sharing a story, it is our responsibility to get to the bottom of it by checking reliable sources. Social media can be a useful starting point, but it should never be our only source of news.

6.title: The Fact-Checking Club's first term

6.briefEs: Escribe un informe sobre el primer trimestre de un club escolar que verifica noticias compartidas en línea: lo hecho, los resultados y recomendaciones.
criteria: Use the present perfect, the present perfect continuous and the simple past correctly (one verb of each at least, with “since”, “for”, “so far” or specific times).
Use at least two past perfect verbs with a time adverb (already, by October, before).

6.model:
Report: The Fact-Checking Club's First Term

Introduction
This report summarises what the Fact-Checking Club has achieved since it was founded in September. It also suggests improvements for next term.

Activities
Members have been meeting every Thursday for twelve weeks. So far, they have checked forty-two stories that students had shared on social media. By October, the club had already discovered that a rumour about cancelled exams was unsubstantiated. In November, two members interviewed an eyewitness who corrected a story about a fight in the playground. The club has also been publishing a weekly list of true and false claims.

Results
Most students have read the list, and many have stopped forwarding unverified messages. Last week alone, three hundred students viewed the list online. However, some students think the club is biased, because it has never corrected stories about the teachers.

Recommendations
The club should try to corroborate every story with two sources and include more teachers' claims. It should also avoid blowing small mistakes out of proportion.

6.title: A request for a correction

6.briefEs: Escribe una carta formal al director de un periódico pidiendo la corrección de un artículo que publicó información falsa sobre tu negocio u organización.

Dear Editor,

I am writing to request a correction to an article that appeared in your newspaper on 14 May under the headline "Local bakery closed after inspection".

The article states that my bakery, Pan y Sol, was closed by the health authorities. This is untrue. The inspectors visited us on 10 May, and they found no problems. The reporter had not contacted us before publishing, and she did not corroborate the story with the inspectors.

Since the article appeared, we have lost many customers, and I have been receiving angry messages every day. The rumour that spread online after publication has been blown out of proportion.

I therefore ask you to publish a correction on the same page, with equal prominence, and to remove the article from your website. I have attached the inspection report as evidence.

6.title: The Moon hoax of 1835
6.brief: Write a magazine article about a famous hoax or false story from history. Explain how it started, how people reacted and what we can learn from it today.
6.briefEs: Escribe un artículo de revista sobre un engaño famoso de la historia: cómo empezó, cómo reaccionó la gente y qué podemos aprender hoy.
criteria: Use the simple past for the events, the present perfect or present perfect continuous for what has happened since, and at least two past perfect verbs.
Use at least three words from the unit (to corroborate, unsubstantiated, to blow out of proportion, rumour, hoax).
Include a title and end with a lesson for today.
6.model:
The Moon Hoax of 1835

In August 1835, a New York newspaper called The Sun published a series of articles that shocked its readers. According to the reports, a famous astronomer, Sir John Herschel, had discovered life on the Moon, including bat-like winged creatures.

The stories were completely false, but many people believed them. The newspaper's sales rose quickly, and other papers copied the news without checking it. Nobody had been to the Moon, and nobody could corroborate the claims. Herschel, who was in South Africa at the time, had never written anything of the kind.

Eventually, it became clear that the series was a hoax. Since then, historians have been using the case as an early example of a story blown out of proportion.

What has changed since 1835? Very little. Rumours have been travelling faster than ever, and unsubstantiated stories still spread widely on social media. The lesson has stayed the same: if a story sounds too amazing to be true, it probably is.

6.title: The Truth Machine: a documentary about fake news
6.brief: Write a review of a documentary, series or book about misinformation. Describe what it shows, say what impressed or disappointed you and give a rating.
6.briefEs: Escribe una reseña de un documental, serie o libro sobre desinformación: qué muestra, qué te impresionó o decepcionó y una valoración.

The Truth Machine: a documentary about fake news

The Truth Machine is a ninety-minute documentary that has been shown on streaming platforms since January. It follows three journalists who have been investigating how false stories spread online.

The film begins with a simple example. In 2019, a photo of a flooded street, which had been edited, was shared thousands of times before anyone checked it. The journalists then trace the image back to its origin and interview an eyewitness who had been standing in the street that day.

What impressed me most was the way the documentary explains why people share rumours: they often do it when they feel angry or afraid. However, I found the film slightly biased, because it only interviews experts who agree with each other. The last twenty minutes also felt repetitive.

Overall, it is a clear, thoughtful introduction to a problem that has been growing for years. I would recommend it to teenagers and adults alike. Four stars out of five.

6.title: A rumour about the bakery
6.brief: Write a short story about a rumour that spread quickly in your school, village or neighbourhood and how it ended.
6.briefEs: Escribe un relato corto sobre un rumor que se extendió rápido en tu colegio, pueblo o barrio y cómo terminó.

It started with a single sentence in a school group chat: "The new supermarket is going to close my grandfather's bakery." By the time I got to school, everybody had already heard it.

My grandfather had been running the bakery for forty years. At lunch, classmates looked at me with sympathy. I called him immediately. "Who told you that?" he laughed. "Nobody has said anything to me."

I spent the afternoon asking around. Nobody knew where the message had come from. A girl had heard it from her cousin, who had heard it from a neighbour. The rumour had been growing all day, and nobody could corroborate it.

By Friday, the story had been blown out of proportion: people were collecting signatures to save the bakery. Eventually, the supermarket manager visited my grandfather and explained that the company simply wanted to sell his bread.

I have been wondering ever since how a single sentence can travel so far. Now, before forwarding anything, I ask myself: has anybody checked this?

6.title: An unverified claim in the newsletter

7.title: Should social media be regulated?
7.brief: Write an essay discussing whether governments should regulate social media platforms more strictly.
7.briefEs: Escribe un ensayo sobre si los gobiernos deberían regular más las redes sociales.
criteria: Two negative questions to introduce opinions (Isn’t it true that…? Shouldn’t we…?).
Three passives in present continuous, present perfect or future (is being debated, has been introduced, will be rolled out).
Four words from the unit: misinformation, echo chamber, data privacy, addictive.
7.model:
Social media has transformed communication, but it has also created new problems. Today, the regulation of these platforms is being debated in parliaments all over the world.

Supporters of regulation point to the spread of misinformation. Isn't it true that false stories have influenced elections in several countries? Many users live in echo chambers, where they only see opinions similar to their own. In addition, data privacy is a serious concern: our personal information has been collected and sold for years, often without our real consent. Some laws have been introduced in Europe, and similar rules will probably be rolled out in Latin America soon.

On the other hand, critics argue that too much regulation could threaten freedom of expression. Who decides what is true and what is false? Governments could use these laws to silence journalists or opponents.

In my view, some regulation is necessary, especially to protect children from addictive designs and to make companies responsible for harmful content. Shouldn't platforms that earn billions be held accountable? However, any new laws must be transparent and must be supervised by independent bodies, not by politicians alone.

7.title: A digital detox
7.brief: Write an article about a week without your phone or the internet. Describe the experience and what you learned.
7.briefEs: Escribe un artículo sobre una semana sin celular o internet: la experiencia y lo que aprendiste.

My Week Offline

We all check our phones first thing in the morning, don't we? I certainly did — until last month, when I decided to log off for a whole week.

Before the experiment, I was glued to a screen for about seven hours a day. I felt I had to keep up with every message, every piece of news and every friend's story. It's exhausting, isn't it?

The first two days were horrible. I kept reaching for my phone in my pocket, and I felt anxious about missing something important. But by Wednesday, something changed. I started reading a novel, I went for long walks and I actually talked to the people on the bus. I even slept better.

When the week finished, I had 400 unread messages. Guess what? Almost none of them were urgent. 

Since then, I've changed my habits. I switch off notifications after 8 p.m. and I never take my phone to bed. You've thought about trying something similar, haven't you? I recommend it — even a weekend can make a difference.

7.title: A proposal for phone rules at school

Proposal: Mobile Phone Use at Green Valley School

Finally, wouldn't it be wise to involve parents? A short guide will be sent home so that families can apply similar rules.

7.title: Voxa Mini: a smart speaker that listens a little too much?

7.title: Is artificial intelligence making students lazy?
7.brief: Write an argumentative essay on whether artificial intelligence tools are making students lazy. Give arguments for both sides and your opinion.
7.briefEs: Escribe un ensayo argumentativo sobre si las herramientas de inteligencia artificial vuelven perezosos a los estudiantes, con argumentos de ambos lados y tu opinión.
criteria: Use at least two negative questions to introduce opinions and at least one tag question.
Use at least four passive forms in different tenses (are used, is being completed, has been made, will be corrected).
Organise the essay in an introduction, two body paragraphs and a conclusion with your opinion.
7.model:
Artificial intelligence tools are now used by millions of students, aren't they? Essays can be written in seconds, and homework is being completed by chatbots. Some teachers fear that students are becoming lazy. Is this fear justified?

On the one hand, it is true that learning has been made too easy. If an answer is generated instantly, why should anyone think? Isn't it obvious that skills which are not practised are quickly lost?

On the other hand, these tools can be used responsibly. A student whose questions are answered patiently can understand a topic faster, and mistakes will be corrected immediately. Calculators were also criticised when they were introduced, weren't they? Yet nobody today thinks that maths has been destroyed.

In my view, the problem is not the technology but the way it is used. Schools should teach students to ask questions rather than copy answers. If homework is designed carefully, AI will be seen as a tutor, not a shortcut.

7.title: The night the internet went down

At exactly seven o'clock on Saturday evening, the internet in our neighbourhood was cut off. Nothing could be streamed, and no messages could be sent. My sister and I looked at each other in horror. We had been planning a film night, and the film had not been downloaded.

"It'll come back soon, won't it?" she asked. It didn't. After an hour, I had checked my phone forty times.

Then my father found a box in the cupboard. A board game that had not been played for years was brought to the table. At first, we complained. Gradually, however, the house was filled with laughter. My mother, who is usually glued to her tablet, won twice.

Around ten, the connection was restored, but nobody noticed until the next morning. "We should do this again, shouldn't we?" my father said over breakfast.

I didn't miss the internet that evening at all. Isn't it strange how much can be gained by disconnecting?

8.title: How to improve your memory
8.brief: Write an article for a student website with practical advice on improving memory. Explain how the brain stores information.
8.briefEs: Escribe un artículo con consejos prácticos para mejorar la memoria y cómo el cerebro guarda información.

Two sentence-modifying “which” clauses (…, which means that…).

8.model:
Five Ways to Boost Your Memory

We've all been there: you sit down in an exam and draw a blank. The good news is that memory is a skill, and it can be improved.

1. Space your learning. Information studied over several days is retained much better than information crammed the night before, which explains why last-minute studying rarely works.

2. Sleep well. During sleep, the brain transfers new information to long-term memory. Students staying up all night are actually making it harder for facts to sink in.

3. Teach someone else. Explaining a topic in your own words forces you to grasp the main ideas, which makes you notice what you don't understand yet.

4. Use associations. Images, songs and stories linked to new words can jog your memory when you need them. That's why people with a knack for languages often create funny mental pictures.

5. Test yourself. Rereading notes feels productive, but questions answered without looking at your book build stronger connections.

Don't rack your brains trying to remember everything at once. Small, regular habits make a huge difference to your retention.

My father has always been absent-minded, but last Sunday was a record.

He woke up early to prepare a surprise breakfast for my mother's birthday. First, he left the house to buy bread and forgot his wallet, which meant he had to come back. Then he couldn't remember the name of the cake my mother loves. "It's on the tip of my tongue," he kept saying, standing in the bakery for ten minutes.

When he got home, the coffee machine was still on, which had filled the kitchen with a terrible smell. He had also forgotten the eggs boiling on the stove! The guests arriving at noon found him opening all the windows.

The worst part came at lunch. When my aunt asked him what present he had bought, his face went white. It had completely slipped his mind!

Luckily, my mother has a great sense of humour. She laughed and said the best present was the story, which we still tell at every family party.

8.title: Learning styles: myth or reality?
8.brief: Some people say everyone has a learning style (visual, auditory, kinaesthetic). Write an essay giving your opinion with arguments.
8.briefEs: Escribe un ensayo de opinión sobre si existen los estilos de aprendizaje (visual, auditivo, kinestésico).
criteria: Three reduced relative clauses.
Two sentence-modifying “which” clauses.
Use “to grasp”, “retention” and “to mull over”.
8.model:
Many teachers believe that every student has a preferred learning style, and that lessons should be adapted to it. Although this idea is popular, research suggests that it is more complicated.

The theory says that visual learners grasp information through images, while auditory learners prefer listening, and kinaesthetic learners need movement. Teachers using this approach often give students questionnaires to discover their style, which seems logical and student-centred.

However, scientists have found little evidence to support the theory. In several studies, students taught in their "preferred" style did not remember more than students taught in other ways, which suggests that the idea may be a myth. What seems to matter is the type of content: maps are best learned visually, and pronunciation is best learned by listening, whatever a person's preferences.

Having mulled over the arguments, I believe that it is more useful to combine different methods for everyone. Lessons including images, discussion and practical activities improve retention for all students. Labelling learners as "visual" or "auditory" might actually limit them. Instead, we should help students discover which strategies work best for each task.

8.title: Study techniques of Year 12 students

Report: Study Techniques of Year 12 Students

Introduction
This report analyses the study techniques of seventy Year 12 students, based on a questionnaire completed in October. The results are presented below, together with some practical suggestions.

Findings
Students preparing for exams mostly reread their notes, which is the least effective method according to recent research. Few of those interviewed use self-testing, although the students who do so score higher in class tests. Information studied the night before is quickly forgotten, which explains why many students draw a blank in exams. Pupils using flashcards said that new vocabulary sank in more easily.

Recommendations
Teachers should introduce techniques based on self-testing, such as quizzes given at the start of lessons. Students should also be encouraged to space their revision over several days, which helps information to be stored in long-term memory.

Conclusion
Changing study habits takes time, which is why the school should start early in the year. A small investment of time now could improve results by the summer.

8.title: A smell from the past
8.brief: Write a short story about a moment when a smell, a song or an object suddenly brought back a memory.

It was a Tuesday, and I was standing in a supermarket queue when it happened. A woman walking past me was wearing a perfume that I had not smelled for twenty years. Suddenly, I was seven again.

I could see my grandmother's kitchen in Pasto, with the blue tiles covering the walls and the radio playing old songs. I could hear her humming while stirring a pot of soup, which smelled of corn and cheese. The memory was extremely clear. I could not even remember what I had eaten for breakfast that morning, which made it even more surprising.

I followed the woman out of the shop, but she had already disappeared. Standing in the car park, I felt a mixture of sadness and joy. The name of the perfume was on the tip of my tongue.

9.title: Generalising about cultures
9.brief: Are stereotypes ever useful? Write an essay discussing the dangers and possible uses of cultural generalisations.
9.briefEs: Escribe un ensayo sobre si los estereotipos culturales son útiles o peligrosos.
criteria: Four contrast and exception expressions (except for, unlike, while, apart from, although).
Use “stereotype”, “to generalise” and “to paint with a broad brush”.
Introduction, two body paragraphs and a conclusion.
9.model:
We often hear statements like "Colombians are always late" or "Germans have no sense of humour". Such stereotypes are everywhere, but are they ever useful?

Some people argue that generalisations can help us understand other cultures. By and large, people from the same country share certain customs and values, which are the result of their upbringing. Knowing, for example, that punctuality is very important in Japan can help a visitor avoid embarrassing situations. Unlike a stereotype, this kind of cultural knowledge is based on research rather than prejudice.

However, the dangers are clear. When we paint a whole nation with a broad brush, we ignore individual differences. Apart from being unfair, stereotypes can be harmful: Colombians who travel abroad often face jokes about drugs, although the vast majority have nothing to do with crime. Deep-rooted stereotypes can also influence decisions about jobs and visas.

In conclusion, while it is natural to generalise, we should be careful. Cultural norms can be a useful starting point, except when they make us stop seeing people as individuals. Every person we meet deserves to be judged on their own merits.

Christmas was magical. My mother would make buñuelos and natilla, and we would sing villancicos for nine nights. I used to believe that Baby Jesus brought the presents, and I would leave a letter under my bed in December.

10.title: How to complain effectively

criteria: Three indirect questions as examples of polite language.
Two noun clauses (What you need to do is…, The fact that…).
Use “to stand your ground”, “to escalate” and “to take something up with someone”.
10.model:
The Art of Complaining

Nobody likes complaining, but sometimes it's necessary. The good news is that a polite, well-prepared complaint is far more effective than an angry one.

First, stay calm. Shouting may make you feel better, but it rarely gets results. What you need to do is explain the problem clearly and briefly: what happened, when, and what you expect. Indirect questions sound much more polite than direct demands. Instead of "Why is my order late?", try "Could you tell me why my order hasn't arrived?" or "I was wondering whether you could check the status of my order."

Second, know what you want. The fact that you are angry is not enough; you need to say if you want a refund, a replacement or an apology. 

Third, keep records. Write down the names of the people you speak to and save every email.

If the first person can't help, ask, "Do you know who I could speak to about this?" and take it up with a manager. Stand your ground, but stay respectful. Only escalate the complaint to a consumer organisation when other options have failed. Remember: you're trying to solve a problem, not win a fight.

10.title: Should refunds for faulty goods be guaranteed?
10.brief: Write an argumentative essay on whether companies should be legally required to give refunds for faulty products without asking questions.

Use at least three noun clauses (What frustrates customers most is that…, The fact that…).

10.model:
Every consumer has experienced a faulty product at some point. Should companies be legally required to give a refund within thirty days, without asking questions? In my opinion, they should, although some conditions are reasonable.

The main argument in favour is fairness. What frustrates customers most is that they often have to prove that they did not cause the fault. Many people give up because they do not know how to ask for redress or whom to approach. A clear rule would protect them, and it would save time for everybody.

However, businesses have legitimate concerns. A small shop may wonder whether customers will abuse the system, for example by buying a dress, wearing it once and returning it. The fact that some people behave dishonestly cannot be ignored.

On balance, I believe the law should guarantee refunds for faulty goods while allowing companies to refuse returns that show clear signs of use. In this way, honest customers would be treated fairly, and shops would still be protected.

Instead of a refund, he gave me new headphones and a discount voucher as a goodwill gesture. What I remember most is that he thanked me for explaining the problem politely.

11.title: What would you do?
11.brief: Write an essay about a moral dilemma: “If you found a wallet with a lot of money and no ID, would you keep it?” Discuss what people would do and why.
11.briefEs: Escribe un ensayo sobre un dilema moral: ¿qué harías si encontraras una billetera con dinero y sin identificación?
criteria: Four present unreal conditionals (If I found…, I would…).

Use “integrity”, “dilemma”, “to draw the line” and “scruples”.
11.model:
Imagine walking down the street and finding a wallet with two million pesos and no identification. What would you do? This classic dilemma reveals a lot about our values.

Some people would keep the money without hesitation. They would argue that, if there were no way to find the owner, nobody would be harmed. Others would keep it because they have serious financial problems. If I were unemployed and couldn't pay my rent, I might be tempted too.

However, most people with integrity would try to return it. If I found the wallet, I would take it to the nearest police station or shop, because the owner might come back to look for it. Even if nobody ever claimed it, I would feel uncomfortable spending money that wasn't mine. For me, this is where I draw the line: a person's moral compass shouldn't depend on whether someone is watching.

Interestingly, a famous experiment in 2019 found that people were more likely to return wallets that contained money. I wish everyone had the same scruples, but the study suggests that most people are more honest than we think.

I also wish I could speak to my grandmother in her language, Wayuunaiki, which I never learned as a child. I wish I had asked her to teach me when I was younger, but I didn't value it then.

I've had second thoughts about many decisions, but I've learned something important. Regrets are useful only if they change the way we act. Now, when I see someone being treated unfairly, I speak up.

Imagine you see your best friend copying answers during an important exam. Would you tell the teacher? This dilemma tests our loyalty and our sense of honesty.

On the other hand, I would not report him immediately. If I were in that situation, I would speak to him after the exam and ask him to confess. He would have the chance to correct his mistake, and our friendship might survive. If he refused, I would draw the line and inform the teacher.

Some people would say that reporting a friend shows a lack of loyalty. I wish things were that simple. However, if I stayed silent, my own integrity would suffer, and I would regret it later.

12 Angry Men: a lesson in doing the right thing

12 Angry Men is a 1957 film directed by Sidney Lumet. Almost the whole story takes place in one hot room, where twelve jurors must decide whether a teenager is guilty of murder. At the start, eleven of them vote guilty. Only one, played by Henry Fonda, has doubts.

What makes the film special is the moral dilemma. If you were that juror, would you risk the anger of the group to defend a stranger? I often asked myself that question while watching. The film suggests that integrity sometimes means standing alone, and I wish more people had that courage.

The acting is superb, and the tension grows slowly. If the film were longer, it might become repetitive, but it lasts only ninety-six minutes. My only criticism is that the characters are all men, which feels dated today.

When Marta heard that she was being considered for the position of team leader, she could hardly believe it. If she got the job, she would earn more money and finally move to a bigger flat. Then her friend Julián asked her for a favour.

Moving to Bogotá: A Survival Guide for Expats

Moving to a new country is an adventure, but it can also be overwhelming. Here are some tips to help you settle in.

Dealing with red tape
Colombian bureaucracy can be frustrating. Apply for your visa and your foreign ID (cédula de extranjería) as soon as possible, and always bring photocopies of everything. Be patient: some procedures take weeks.

Getting around
Bogotá's traffic is famous, and not for good reasons. Download a ride app and learn how the TransMilenio works. Many expats also buy a bike, as the city has more than 500 km of cycle paths.

Acclimatising
At 2,600 metres above sea level, the altitude can make you tired for the first few days. Drink water and take it easy. The weather changes constantly, so always carry an umbrella and a jacket.

Culture shock and homesickness
Almost everyone feels homesick at some point. Join expat groups, but also make Colombian friends — they are usually very welcoming. By your third month, you will have learned the basics of the local slang, and by the end of the year, you will have become a real rolo!

But she stayed. Slowly, she settled in. She found a job in a bakery, learned French at night school and met people who became her second family. Today, she owns a small café that sells Colombian coffee and pandebono. By next June, she will have been living in Canada for eight years.

Sometimes, on cold mornings, she wonders how life would be if she had stayed in Colombia. If she hadn't moved, she would probably be working in her father's shop now. She wouldn't speak three languages. If she had returned during that first winter, she wouldn't have her café today, and she wouldn't be married to Luc, who she met there.

"Leaving was the hardest decision of my life," she says. "But if I hadn't taken that risk, I wouldn't be the person I am now."

If I hadn't taken that job, I would not be so interested in sustainable energy today. It has broadened my horizons, and I now feel ready for a fresh start abroad.

I would be grateful if you could tell me what the entry requirements are and whether scholarships are available for international students. I would also like to know whether the university offers help with accommodation, since I imagine I might feel like a fish out of water at first.

I understand that visa procedures involve a lot of red tape, so any guidance on the documents I will need would be very helpful. By the end of this month, I will have gathered all my certificates.

12.title: Brooklyn: a story about leaving home
12.brief: Write a review of a film or book about someone who moves to another country. Describe the story, say what you liked and give a rating. B2+ / puente a C1 (future perfect continuous).
12.briefEs: Escribe una reseña de una película o libro sobre alguien que emigra: la historia, lo que te gustó y una valoración. B2+ / puente a C1 (futuro perfecto continuo).
criteria: Use at least one mixed conditional (If she had stayed…, she would not be…) and one future perfect continuous (By the time the credits roll, you will have been…).
Use at least three words or expressions from the unit (a fish out of water, homesick, to settle in, to put down roots).
Express your opinion clearly and end with a rating.
12.model:
Brooklyn: a story about leaving home

Brooklyn (2015) is a quiet, beautifully acted drama set in the 1950s. Eilis, a young Irish woman played by Saoirse Ronan, leaves her small town for New York, where she feels like a fish out of water.

What I liked most is how realistically the film shows the process of settling in. Slowly, Eilis makes friends, finds a job in a department store and falls in love. By the end of the first year, she has put down roots in a new country. If she had stayed in Ireland, she would not be the confident woman we see at the end.

The film then asks a difficult question: where is home? When a family emergency takes her back to Ireland, she must decide whether to stay or return.

My only criticism is that the pace is slow, which may disappoint viewers who like action. By the time the credits roll, you will have been rooting for her for two hours. Overall, it is a warm and honest film, and I give it four out of five stars.

12.title: Settling in at the Medellín branch
12.brief: Write a report on how foreign employees have adapted to a new branch abroad. Present the findings and recommend support for future arrivals.
12.briefEs: Escribe un informe sobre cómo se han adaptado los empleados extranjeros a una nueva sede: presenta los hallazgos y recomienda apoyo para los próximos que lleguen.
criteria: Use at least two future perfect forms, including one future perfect continuous (will have been living).
Use one mixed or present unreal conditional (If new staff had received this support earlier, they would feel…).
Use at least three words from the unit (culture shock, homesick, red tape, to put down roots, to settle in) and the headings Introduction, Findings, Recommendations and Conclusion.
12.model:
Report: Settling in at the Medellín Branch

Introduction
This report examines how the twelve foreign employees who joined our Medellín branch this year have adapted, and suggests ways of helping future arrivals.

Findings
Most employees said that culture shock was stronger than they had expected. Some felt homesick during the first two months, and several were overwhelmed by the red tape required to obtain a residence permit. By December, nine of them will have been living in the city for a full year, and most say they have put down roots. Employees who had been given a local mentor settled in faster than those who had not.

Recommendations
The company should provide a mentor for every newcomer and a guide explaining the paperwork. A short welcome event in the first week would also help people meet colleagues. If new staff had received this support earlier, they would feel less isolated now.

Conclusion
By next spring, we will have welcomed another fifteen employees, so these improvements should be in place by then.

12.title: An orientation programme for international students

12.briefEs: Escribe una propuesta a una universidad para un programa de orientación que ayude a estudiantes internacionales a adaptarse: situación actual y lo que habrán logrado al terminar. [B2+ / puente a C1]
criteria: Use at least three future perfect forms, including one future perfect continuous (will have been studying).
Use one mixed or present unreal conditional (If the university had offered more support, they would feel…).
Use at least three expressions from the unit (a fish out of water, culture shock, red tape, to get around, to settle in) and the headings Introduction, Current situation, Proposal and Conclusion.
12.model:
Proposal: An Orientation Programme for International Students

Introduction
This proposal recommends a three-day orientation programme for the international students who will join our university next September.

Current situation
At present, newcomers receive an email with general information and nothing more. Many say they felt like fish out of water during their first weeks. If the university had offered more support, they would probably feel more confident today. Moreover, dealing with red tape is a common source of stress, especially for students who have never lived abroad.

Proposal
We suggest a programme including a campus tour, workshops on culture shock and a session on getting around the city. By the end of the third day, participants will have met their mentors and will have opened a local bank account. Mentors, who would be current students, would stay in contact for the first semester.

Conclusion
By the end of the first term, students will have been studying here for three months, and we hope they will have settled in comfortably.

12.title: Is studying abroad worth it?
12.brief: Write an argumentative essay on whether studying abroad is worth the cost and the difficulties. Present both sides and give your opinion. [B2+ / puente a C1]
12.briefEs: Escribe un ensayo argumentativo sobre si estudiar en el extranjero vale el costo y las dificultades. Presenta ambos lados y da tu opinión. [B2+ / puente a C1]
criteria: Use at least three future perfect forms, including one future perfect continuous or perfect form with “by the time”.
Use one mixed conditional (If I hadn’t spent a year in Canada, I would not be…).

Use at least three expressions from the unit (to broaden one’s horizons, culture shock, a fish out of water, a fresh start) and organise the essay in an introduction, two body paragraphs and a conclusion.
12.model:
Every year, thousands of young people leave their home countries to study abroad. Is the experience worth the cost and the difficulties?

On the one hand, living in another country can change a person. By the time students return, they will have been immersed in a foreign language for months, and they will have learned to solve problems alone. Studying abroad broadens horizons in a way that no textbook can. If I hadn't spent a year in Canada, I would not be as independent as I am now.

On the other hand, the difficulties are real. Culture shock and homesickness can be so severe that some students give up. Students who feel like a fish out of water may not enjoy the experience at all.

In my opinion, the benefits outweigh the risks, provided that students receive support when they arrive. By the end of their first year abroad, most will have found a fresh start and will have grown in ways they never imagined.
